/** Generate token */
public static String generateToken(Map<String, Object> claimMaps) {

    if (null != claimMaps) {
        claimMaps.forEach((key, val) -> {
            claimMaps.put(key, val.toString());
        });
    }

    return Jwts.builder()
            // JWT_ID, can be used for unique identification of each signature
            .setId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
            // Data compression method
            .compressWith(CompressionCodecs.GZIP)
            // Issuer information
            .setIssuer(ISSUER)
            // Subject
            .setSubject("system")
            // Audience
            .setAudience(AUDIENCE)
            // Issued-at timestamp
            .setIssuedAt(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis()))
            // Expiration timestamp
            .setExpiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + EXPIRES_IN * 1000))
            // Claim information, custom payload
            .addClaims(claimMaps)
            // Signature algorithm + secret key
            .signWith(SIGNATURE_ALGORITHM, secretKey)
            .compact();
}

The process of verifying a token is essentially the same as generating a new token.

Based on the received header, payload, and the secret key stored on the server, a new token is regenerated and compared:

  • If the tokens match, the token is valid and has not been tampered with.
  • If the token has not been tampered with, the payload can be further decrypted via Base64, and the exp expiration field in the payload can be used to determine whether the token has expired.

Note: JWT itself contains authentication information, so once the information is leaked, anyone can obtain all the permissions of the token. Therefore, when doing front-end development, it is best not to store JWT in Cookie, which is a storage unit prone to leaking personal privacy information.

Advantages

  • Stateless & Scalable: Very suitable for distributed systems and microservice architectures;
  • Solves Session Sharing Issues: No need to share session storage;
  • Natively supports cross-domain and mobile;
  • Reduces database pressure: Authentication information is built into the token, eliminating the need for frequent database queries.

Disadvantages and Risks

  1. Cannot actively revoke tokens Once issued, a token remains valid until it expires. If a user logs out or their permissions change, the server cannot immediately invalidate the old token (unless a blacklist mechanism is introduced, but this goes against the stateless design principle).
  2. Risk of sensitive information leakage Although the Payload is Base64-encoded, it is not encrypted (unless JWE is used). Never store sensitive data such as passwords in the token.
  3. HTTPS is mandatory JWT is transmitted over the network. If HTTP is used, it is highly susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks. Always use HTTPS throughout.
  4. Large token size Compared to traditional session IDs, JWT is longer because it contains data, which may affect performance (especially in high-frequency request scenarios).

Additional Notes

  • Single Sign-On (SSO): JWT natively supports SSO because the token can be verified by multiple services.

  • Homepage Access Control: If you need to “open the homepage” (i.e., allow anonymous access), you should configure a whitelist path in the gateway or interceptor to skip JWT verification.

  • Cross-domain Support: JWT itself is not related to CORS, but when used with the Authorization Header, cross-domain authentication can be easily achieved.

  • Comparison with Spring Session:

    • Spring Session relies on server-side storage (e.g., Redis) and supports active invalidation;
    • JWT is stateless but sacrifices real-time control capability;
    • Both are suitable for different scenarios and can be used in combination (e.g., using JWT for authentication and Redis for managing blacklists).

Recommended Approaches for Enhancing JWT Security and Controllability

Although JWT has advantages such as being stateless and scalable, its characteristic of “inability to actively revoke” does pose challenges in certain business scenarios (such as user logout, password changes, permission changes). To address this, the following two complementary strategies are recommended to enhance the system’s security control capabilities:

Approach 1: Short-lived Access Token + Refresh Token Mechanism

  • Core Idea:

    • Access Token: Has a short validity period (e.g., 15–30 minutes), used for everyday API authentication;
    • Refresh Token: Has a longer validity period (e.g., 7 days), stored in a secure HttpOnly Cookie or secure storage, used only to obtain a new Access Token.

  • Workflow:

    1. After the user successfully logs in, the server returns a pair of tokens: access_token and refresh_token;
    2. The client uses the access_token to call protected APIs;
    3. When the access_token expires, the client uses the refresh_token to request a new access_token from the authentication service;
    4. If the user logs out or changes their password, the server immediately revokes the corresponding refresh_token (e.g., deletes it from the database or Redis);
    5. Even if the old access_token has not yet expired, since it cannot be renewed, the effective window is greatly shortened.

  • Advantages:

    • Balances security and user experience;
    • After logout, the token becomes fully invalid at most after one Access Token lifecycle (e.g., 30 minutes);
    • Conforms to OAuth 2.0 standard practices.

Approach 2: Lightweight Token Blacklist / Whitelist Mechanism Based on Redis

  • Implementation A: JTI Blacklist

    • Embed a unique identifier in the JWT’s jti (JWT ID) field;
    • When a user logs out, changes password, or has permission changes, store the jti and its expiration time in Redis (TTL = remaining validity period of the original JWT);
    • Each time a JWT is verified, additionally check whether the jti exists in the blacklist;
    • If it exists, reject the request.

  • Implementation B: User Session Whitelist (Stricter)

    • After each successful login generates a JWT, store the full token string (or its hash value) in Redis keyed by user_id:session_id;
    • All protected APIs, after verifying the JWT signature and expiration, additionally verify whether the token exists in Redis;
    • When a user logs out, changes password, or an administrator forces an offline, delete the corresponding Redis key;
    • At this point, even if the token has not expired and the signature is valid, it will be rejected because it is “not in the whitelist.”

  • Advantages:

    • Achieves true instant logout;
    • Supports fine-grained control (e.g., multi-device management, forced logout);
    • Redis offers high performance with minimal impact on system throughput.

  • Notes:

    • Properly set the TTL of Redis keys to avoid unlimited memory growth;
    • While the whitelist approach is more secure, it slightly sacrifices JWT’s “fully stateless” nature, belonging to a stateful enhancement pattern.

Comprehensive Recommendations

Scenario Recommended Approach
General Web applications, mobile Apps Access Token + Refresh Token (balances security and performance)
High-security systems (e.g., finance, admin panels) Refresh Token + Redis Blacklist/Whitelist
Need to support “multi-device login management” Use Redis Whitelist + session_id to identify devices

💡 Best Practice: Even when using a blacklist mechanism, keep the Access Token’s validity period short (e.g., ≤30 minutes) to limit Redis storage pressure and potential attack windows.

ThreadLocal Introduction

From the official Java documentation: The ThreadLocal class is used to provide thread-local variables. These variables, when accessed in a multithreaded environment (via get and set methods), ensure that each thread’s variables are relatively independent from variables in other threads. ThreadLocal instances are typically private static types, used to associate threads with their context.

We can understand ThreadLocal’s purpose as: providing thread-local variables that don’t interfere with each other between different threads. These variables are effective within a thread’s lifecycle, reducing the complexity of passing common variables between multiple functions or components within the same thread.

  • Thread concurrency: In multithreaded concurrent scenarios
  • Data passing: We can use ThreadLocal to pass common variables between different components within the same thread (somewhat similar to Session?)
  • Thread isolation: Each thread’s variables are independent and don’t affect each other

Basic Usage

Application Scenarios

Transfer Example

Let’s construct a simple transfer scenario: there’s an account table with two users, Jack and Rose, where user Jack transfers money to user Rose. The implementation uses MySQL database, JDBC, and C3P0 framework. Here’s the detailed code

Introducing Transactions

In multithreaded scenarios, each thread can only operate on its own connection - thread isolation.

Conventional Solutions

  • Passing Connection objects from service layer to DAO layer

  • Reduces program performance (synchronized code blocks lose concurrency)

This is where ThreadLocal can bind to the current thread to reduce code coupling

Using ThreadLocal Solution

  • Change from retrieving objects from connection pool to directly getting the current thread’s bound connection object

    • Bind this connection object to current thread

    return conn;
}

ThreadLocal Implementation Benefits

From the above case, we can see that in specific scenarios, ThreadLocal solution has two prominent advantages:

  • Data passing: Saves data bound to each thread, can be retrieved directly where needed, avoiding code coupling from direct parameter passing
  • Thread isolation: Data between threads is isolated yet concurrent, avoiding performance loss from synchronization methods

ThreadLocal Internal Structure

Through the above learning, we’ve understood ThreadLocal’s functionality. Now let’s examine ThreadLocal’s internal structure to explore the principle behind its thread data isolation.

Common Misconceptions

Without examining the source code, one might guess ThreadLocal is designed like this: each ThreadLocal creates a Map, using the thread as Map’s key and the local variable to store as Map’s value, achieving local variable isolation for each thread. This is the simplest design method, and JDK’s earliest ThreadLocal was indeed designed this way, but it’s no longer the case.

Current Design

However, JDK later optimized the design. In JDK 8, ThreadLocal’s design is: each Thread maintains a ThreadLocalMap, where this Map’s key is the ThreadLocal instance itself, and value is the actual object to store. The specific process is:

  • Each Thread has an internal Map (ThreadLocalMap)
  • Map stores ThreadLocal objects (key) and thread variable copies (value)
  • Thread’s internal Map is maintained by ThreadLocal, which is responsible for getting and setting thread variable values from the map
  • For different threads, when retrieving copy values, other threads cannot access the current thread’s copy value, forming copy isolation without interference

Comparison

What are the benefits of JDK8’s design?

  • Each Map stores fewer Entry数量, as original Entry count was determined by Thread, now determined by ThreadLocal
    • In real development, Thread count far exceeds ThreadLocal count
  • When Thread is destroyed, ThreadLocalMap is also destroyed, as ThreadLocal is stored within Thread, disappearing with Thread destruction, reducing overhead.

ThreadLocal Core Method Source Code

Based on ThreadLocal’s internal structure, we continue analyzing its core method source code for deeper understanding of its operational principles. Besides constructors, ThreadLocal exposes the following 4 methods

Method Declaration Description
protected T initialValue() Return initial value of current thread’s local variable
public void set(T value) Return current thread’s bound local variable
public T get() Get current thread’s bound local variable
public void remove() Remove current thread’s bound local variable

Below is detailed source code analysis of these 4 methods (ThreadLocalMap section temporarily omitted for clarity, to be detailed in next knowledge point)

set Method

Code flow

  • First get current thread, and based on current thread get a Map
  • If retrieved Map is not empty, set parameter to Map (using current ThreadLocal reference as key)
  • If Map is empty, create Map for that thread and set initial value

get Method

Code execution flow

  • First get current thread, based on current thread get a Map
  • If retrieved Map is not empty, use ThreadLocal reference as key to get corresponding Entry from Map, otherwise go to step 4
  • If e is not null, return e.value, otherwise go to step 4
  • Map is empty or e is empty, get initial value via initialValue function, then create new Map using ThreadLocal reference and value as firstKey and firstValue

Summary: First get current thread’s ThreadLocal variable, if exists return value, if not exists create and return initial value

remove Method

Code execution flow

  • First get current thread, based on current thread get a Map
  • If retrieved Map is not empty, remove Entry corresponding to current ThreadLocal object

initialValue Method

This method returns the initial value of the thread-local variable.

  • This method is a lazy invocation method. From the above code, we see it executes when set hasn’t been called but get is called first, and only executes once.
  • This method’s default implementation directly returns null.
  • To get an initial value other than null, override this method. (Note: this is a protected method, obviously designed for subclass overriding)

When analyzing ThreadLocal methods, we learned that ThreadLocal operations actually revolve around ThreadLocalMap. ThreadLocalMap’s source code is relatively complex, we’ll discuss from the following three aspects.

Basic Structure

ThreadLocalMap is ThreadLocal’s inner class, doesn’t implement Map interface, implements Map functionality independently, with its own Entry implementation.

 * Expansion threshold, expands when table usage exceeds this
 **/
private int threshold; // Default to 0

Similar to HashMap, INITIAL_CAPACITY represents Map’s initial capacity; table is an Entry-type array for storing data; size represents stored count; threshold represents size threshold for expansion.

Storage Structure - Entry

/*
 *Entry inherits WeakReference, uses ThreadLocal as key.
 If key is null (entry.get()==null), key is no longer referenced,
 *therefore entry can be cleared from table.
 */
static class Entry extends WeakReference<ThreadLocal<?>>{

    Object value; Entry(ThreadLocal<?> k, Object v) {
    super(k);
    value = v;
}}

In ThreadLocalMap, Entry also stores K-V structured data. However, Entry’s key can only be ThreadLocal object, as limited in the constructor.

Additionally, Entry inherits WeakReference, meaning key (ThreadLocal) is weakly referenced, aimed at decoupling ThreadLocal object’s lifecycle from thread lifecycle.

Weak References and Memory Leaks

Some developers discover memory leaks when using ThreadLocal, guessing this relates to weak reference keys in Entry. This understanding is actually incorrect.

Let’s review the concepts involved in this problem before analyzing.

Memory Leak Related Concepts

Memory overflow: Insufficient memory for applicants.

Memory leak: Dynamically allocated heap memory in programs not released or unable to be released due to some reason, causing system memory waste, leading to slower program execution or even system crashes. Accumulated memory leaks will eventually cause memory overflow.

Weak Reference Related Concepts

Java has 4 reference types: strong, soft, weak, and phantom. This problem mainly involves strong and weak references:

Strong Reference (“Strong” Reference): The most common object reference. As long as a strong reference points to an object, the object is considered “alive” and garbage collector won’t collect it.

Weak Reference (WeakReference): Once garbage collector discovers objects with only weak references, regardless of current memory space availability, it will reclaim their memory.

If key uses strong reference, will memory leak occur?

Assuming ThreadLocalMap’s key uses strong reference, will memory leak occur?

ThreadLocal memory diagram at this point (solid lines represent strong references):

  • Assuming business code finishes using ThreadLocal, threadLocal Ref is collected
  • But because threadLocalMap’s Entry has strong reference to threadLocal, threadLocal cannot be collected.
  • Without manually deleting this Entry and CurrentThread still running, there’s always a strong reference chain threadRef->currentThread->threadLocalMap->entry, Entry won’t be collected (Entry includes ThreadLocal instance and value), causing Entry memory leak.

This means ThreadLocalMap’s key using strong reference cannot completely avoid memory leaks.

If key uses weak reference, will memory leak occur?

  • Similarly assuming business code finishes using ThreadLocal, threadLocal Ref is collected.
  • Since ThreadLocalMap only holds ThreadLocal’s weak reference, no strong reference points to threadlocal instance, so threadlocal can be smoothly GC collected, at this point Entry’s key=null.
  • But without manually deleting this Entry and CurrentThread still running, there’s also a strong reference chain threadRef->currentThread->threadLocalMap->entry->value, value won’t be collected, and this value will never be accessed, causing value memory leak.

This means ThreadLocalMap’s key using weak reference can also cause memory leaks.

Real Cause of Memory Leaks

Comparing these two situations, we find memory leak occurrence is unrelated to whether ThreadLocalMap’s key uses weak reference. So what’s the real cause of memory leaks?

Careful observers will notice both memory leak situations have two prerequisites:

  • Not manually deleting this Entry
  • CurrentThread still running

The first point is easy to understand - using ThreadLocal’s remove method to delete corresponding Entry after use avoids memory leaks.

The second point is more complex - since ThreadLocalMap is a Thread attribute referenced by current thread, its lifecycle matches Thread’s. After using ThreadLocal, if current Thread also finishes execution, ThreadLocalMap will naturally be GC collected, fundamentally avoiding memory leaks.

In summary, ThreadLocal memory leak root cause is: because ThreadLocalMap’s lifecycle matches Thread’s, not manually deleting corresponding key will cause memory leaks.

Why Use Weak References?

Based on the analysis, we know: regardless of which reference type ThreadLocalMap’s key uses, memory leaks cannot be completely avoided, unrelated to weak reference usage.

Two ways to avoid memory leaks:

  • Using ThreadLocal’s remove method to delete corresponding Entry after use
  • Current Thread also finishes running after using ThreadLocal

Compared to the first method, the second is obviously harder to control, especially with thread pools where threads don’t destroy but return to the pool.

This means as long as you remember to call remove after using ThreadLocal, regardless of whether key is strong or weak reference, there won’t be problems.

So why use weak references for keys?

Actually, in ThreadLocalMap’s set/getEntry methods, when key is null (ThreadLocal is null), it will set value to null.

This means after using ThreadLocal, with CurrentThread still running, even if you forget to call remove, weak references provide an extra guarantee over strong references: weakly referenced ThreadLocal will be collected, corresponding value will be cleared on next ThreadLocalMap set, get, or remove method call, thus avoiding memory leaks.

Hash Conflict Resolution

Hash conflict resolution is an important Map content. Using hash conflict resolution as a clue, let’s study ThreadLocalMap’s core source code.

Starting with ThreadLocal’s set method

public void set(T value) {
    Thread t = Thread.currentThread();
    ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap map = getMap(t);
    if (map != null)
        // Called ThreadLocalMap's set method
        map.set(this, value);
    else
        createMap(t, value);
}

ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap getMap(Thread t) {
    return t.threadLocals;
}

void createMap(Thread t, T firstValue) {
    // Called ThreadLocalMap's constructor
    t.threadLocals = new ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap(this, firstValue);

This method we analyzed earlier - sets current thread’s bound local variable

  • First get current thread, based on current thread get a Map
  • If retrieved Map is not empty, set parameter to Map (using current ThreadLocal reference as key) (here calls ThreadLocalMap’s set method)
  • If Map is empty, create Map for that thread and set initial value (here calls ThreadLocalMap’s constructor)

This code involves two ThreadLocalMap methods, let’s analyze these two methods

Constructor

ThreadLocalMap(ThreadLocal firstKey, Object firstValue)

Constructor first creates Entry array of length 16, then calculates firstKey’s corresponding index, stores to table, sets size and threshold.

Key analysis: int i = firstKey.threadLocalHashCode & (INITIAL_CAPACITY - 1)

About: threadLocalHashCode

Here an AtomicInteger type is defined, each time getting current value plus HASH_INCREMENT, HASH_INCREMENT = 0x61c88647, related to Fibonacci sequence (golden ratio), mainly to ensure hash codes are evenly distributed in 2^n power arrays, i.e., Entry[] table, minimizing hash conflicts.

About & (INITIAL_CAPACITY - 1)

Hash calculation uses hashCode & (size-1) algorithm, equivalent to more efficient hashCode % size modulo operation. Because of this algorithm, size must be power of 2, ensuring minimal hash conflicts while preventing index overflow.

Get Method

Code execution flow

  • First calculate index i based on key, then find Entry at that position,
  • If Entry exists and key equals passed key, directly assign new value to this Entry,
  • If Entry exists but key is null, call replaceStaleEntry to replace this null-keyed Entry,
  • Continuously loop detection until encountering null position, if still no return during loop, create new Entry at this null position, insert, increment size by 1.

Finally call cleanSomeSlots to clean null-keyed Entries, return whether Entries were cleaned, then check if sz >= threshold for rehash conditions, if met call rehash function for full table scan cleanup.

Linear Probing Hash Conflict Resolution

This method probes next address sequentially, inserts when empty address found, overflows if entire space has no empty addresses.

Example: assuming current table length 16, if calculated key hash is 14, if table[14] already has value and its key differs from current key, hash conflict occurs. Then 14+1=15, check table[15], if still conflicts return to 0, check table[0], and so on until insertion possible.

Following the above description, Entry table can be considered a circular array.

ThreadLocal Usage Scenarios

Source Code Usage Scenarios

ThreadLocal’s main function is data isolation, filled data belongs only to current thread, variable data is relatively isolated from other threads, preventing variable tampering by other threads in multithreaded environments.

For example, Spring’s transaction isolation level implementation source code

Spring uses ThreadLocal to ensure single-thread database operations use the same database connection, while enabling business layer to use transactions without perceiving or managing Connection objects, cleverly managing transaction configuration switching, suspension, and recovery through propagation levels.

Spring framework uses ThreadLocal for this isolation, mainly in TransactionSynchronizationManager class, code as follows:

    private static final ThreadLocal<Map<Object, Object>> resources =
            new NamedThreadLocal<>("Transactional resources");

    private static final ThreadLocal<Set<TransactionSynchronization>> synchronizations =
            new NamedThreadLocal<>("Transaction synchronizations");

    private static final ThreadLocal<String> currentTransactionName =
            new NamedThreadLocal<>("Current transaction name");

Spring transactions mainly use ThreadLocal and AOP implementation. I mention here - just know each thread’s own connection is saved via ThreadLocal.

User Usage Scenario 1

Besides source code ThreadLocal usage scenarios, do you have your own usage scenarios?

Previously after launch, we found some users’ dates were incorrect. Investigation revealed SimpleDataFormat was the culprit. When using SimpleDataFormat’s parse() method, internal Calendar object called Calendar.clear() then Calendar.add(). If one thread called add() then another called clear(), the parse() method would parse incorrect time.

Actually solving this is simple - let each thread new its own SimpleDataFormat. But with 1000 threads, should we new 1000 SimpleDataFormats?

So we used thread pool plus ThreadLocal wrapping SimpleDataFormat, calling initialValue to give each thread a SimpleDataFormat copy, solving thread safety issues and improving performance.

User Usage Scenario 2

In my project, there’s a thread frequently encountering cross-method calls requiring context passing - context (Context), a state often representing user identity, task information, etc., causing excessive parameter passing issues.

Similar to chain of responsibility pattern, adding context parameter to every method is cumbersome, and sometimes if call chain has third-party libraries with unmodifiable source code, object parameters can’t be passed. So I used ThreadLocal for transformation - only need to set parameters in ThreadLocal before calls, other places just get.

Why Use Scoop

Scoop Official Website

On Windows, setting up a development environment has always been a complex and difficult problem. Due to the lack of a unified standard, various development environments have vastly different installation methods, requiring a lot of unnecessary time costs. Scoop can help you uniformly install and manage common development software, eliminating the need for manual downloading, installation, and configuring environment variables.

For example, installing Python and Node.js only requires executing:

1
2

scoop install python
scoop install nodejs

Installing Scoop

Tested + Official installation method

Install the latest PowerShell from Microsoft Store

Open PowerShell and enter the following commands

1
2

Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri https://get.scoop.sh | Invoke-Expression

If you see the image below, the installation was successful

Scoop requires Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell as its runtime environment. If you’re using Windows 10 or later, Windows PowerShell is built into the system. However, Windows 7’s built-in Windows PowerShell version is too outdated, and you’ll need to manually install a newer version of PowerShell.

Since many users have set up Windows accounts with Chinese usernames, this causes the user directory to also have a Chinese name. If you install software to the user directory using Scoop’s default method, it may cause some software to execute incorrectly. Therefore, I recommend installing to a custom directory. For other installation methods, please refer to: ScoopInstaller/Install

1
2
3
4
5
6

# Set PowerShell execution policy
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
# Download installation script
irm get.scoop.sh -outfile 'install.ps1'
# Execute installation, --ScoopDir parameter specifies Scoop installation path
.\install.ps1 -ScoopDir 'C:\Scoop'

Using Scoop

Scoop’s official documentation is very beginner-friendly. Rather than repeating information here, I recommend reading the official documentation or Quick Start.

Common Commands

Command Function
scoop bucket list View all currently installed repos
scoop search Used to search software
scoop install Used to install software
scoop list Used to view installed software
scoop uninstall Used to uninstall software
scoop bucket Used to manage repositories
scoop update Used to update software
scoop config proxy Set proxy for scoop
scoop reset Used to switch software versions

Q&A

Can Scoop configure mirror sources?

The Scoop community only maintains installation configurations. All software is downloaded from the official download links provided by the software developers, so mirror sources cannot be provided. If multiple downloads fail due to your network environment, you’ll need a little magic.

Why can’t I find Java8?

For the same reason as above, the official source no longer provides Java8 download links. It’s recommended to use ojdkbuild8 as an alternative.

How do I install Python2?

For deprecated software, the Scoop community removes it from ScoopInstaller/Main and adds it to ScoopInstaller/Versions. If you need these software, you’ll need to manually add the bucket:

1
2

scoop bucket add versions
scoop install python27
